   101	machine $\cal{B}$, even though $\cal{B}$ 
   102	has a different number of input tapes. This is because every
   103	$k$-input Turing machine $\cal{M}$ can be efficiently simulated 
   104	by a single \emph{tape} Turing machine, as given by the following result~\cite{hartmanis1965computational}.
   105	We assume that there is an unambiguous, binary encoding
   106	$\mathrm{enc}_k(x)$ of $k$-tuples $x \in (\{0,1\}^*)^k$ that is computable in
   107	time $O(k + |x_1| + \cdots + |x_k|)$ where $x_i$ is the $i$-th component of the
   108	tuple $x$.\footnote{A canonical choice of such an encoding is the following: a
   109	  tuple $(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ is in encoded into a concatenation of a ``dual rail''
   110	  encoding of each $x_i$: every bit of $x_i$ is expanded via the map $0 \mapsto
   111	  01$, $1 \mapsto 10$, and the end of the string $x_i$ is indicated by $00$.}
   112	 
   113	
   114	
   115	
   116	\begin{theorem}[Efficient universal Turing machine~\cite{hartmanis1965computational}]
   117	  \label{thm:universal-tm}
   118	 For all $k \in \N$ there exists a single tape Turing machine $\cal{U}_k$ (called a \emph{universal Turing machine}) with such
   119	  that for every $x \in (\{0,1\}^*)^k$ and $\alpha \in \{0,1\}^*$, if the tape of 
   120	  the Turing machine $\cal{U}_k$ is initialized with $\mathrm{enc}_{k+1}(\alpha,x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ and 
   121	  $[\alpha]_k$ halts within $T$ steps on input $x$ then $\cal{U}_k$ halts in at most $C(k \cdot |\alpha| \cdot |x| \cdot T)^c$ steps and the contents
   122	    of its tape is $[\alpha]_k(x)$. Here, $C, c \geq 1$ are universal constants, and $|x|$ denotes the sum of lengths $|x_1| + \cdots + |x_k|$. 
   123	    
   124	\end{theorem}
   125	
   126	Thus, the Turing machine $\cal{A}$ can simulate $\cal{B}$ on input $(x,x^2)$ as follows: it first computes
   127	the encoding $\mathrm{enc}_3(\desc{\cal{B}},x,x^2)$ and writes this on a segment of the work tape. Then, it runs
   128	the Turing machine $\cal{U}_k$ from \Cref{thm:universal-tm} on this segment of the work tape, obtaining 
   129	output $y = \cal{B}(x,x^2)$ (if it eventually halts). Then, it writes $y$ onto the output tape of
   130	$\cal{A}$. The total time complexity of $\cal{A}$ on input $x$ then includes the time complexity 
   131	of computing the encoding, running Turing machine $\cal{U}_k$, and writing the final output. 
   132	
   133	We also assume that the length of the canonical description of $\cal{A}$ 
   134	depends only linearly on the canonical description of the Turing machine $\cal{B}$, so that
   135	$|\desc{\cal{A}}| = O(|\desc{\cal{B}}|)$; the constant in the $O(\cdot)$ notation hides
   136	the dependence on the description of the universal Turing machine $\cal{U}_k$, the computation
   137	of the encoding map $\mathrm{enc}_3(\cdot)$, etc. 
   138	
   139	
   140	
   141	
   142	
   143	
   144	\paragraph{Hardwiring constants.} 
   145	Throughout this paper, we often define Turing machines $\cal{M}$
   146	with some number $k$ of inputs, and then for some string $a \in \{0,1\}^*$
   147	define a $(k-1)$-input Turing machine $\cal{M}_a$ whose behavior on input
   148	$(y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$ is to execute $\cal{M}$ on input
   149	$(a,y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$.
   150	Informally, the Turing machine $\cal{M}_a$ ``hardwires'' the input $a$ onto the
   151	first tape of $\cal{M}$.
   152	We  informally write $\cal{M}_a(y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1}) =
   153	\cal{M}(a,y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$.
   154	
   155	More precisely, the Turing machine $\cal{M}_a$ on input $(y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$ first
   156	computes the encoding $e = \mathrm{enc}_{k+1}(\desc{\cal{M}},a,y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$, and then runs the
   157	universal Turing machine $\cal{U}_k$ on input $e$.
   158	The description of $\cal{M}_a$ can be computed from $\desc{\cal{M}}$ and $a$ in
   159	time $O(|a| + |\cal{M}| + O(1))$, where the $O(1)$ comes from the description
   160	length of the universal Turing machine $\cal{U}_k$.
   161	
   162	Furthermore, the time complexity of the Turing machine $\cal{M}_a$ on input
   163	$(y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$ is at most \\ $\poly(|a|,|y_1|,\ldots,|y_{k-1}|,T)$ where $T$
   164	is the time complexity of $\cal{M}$ on input $(a,y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$.
   165	This bound comes from the complexity of encoding the inputs from the $k$ tapes
   166	into the $\mathrm{enc}_{k+1}(\cdot)$ format, and then simulating $\cal{M}$ on input
   167	$(\desc{\cal{M}},a,y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$.
   168	
   169	
   170	
   171	\paragraph{Description complexity bounds.} When we bound the description lengths of
   172	the Turing machines presented in this paper, we do not worry about the exact
   173	details of how Turing machines are represented as binary strings -- as mentioned we assume that
   174	\emph{some} reasonable encoding is used -- but instead
   175	we distinguish between whether the Turing machine 
   176	description depends on any parameters used elsewhere in the paper. Note that whether the \emph{description} depends on any parameters is different from whether the Turing machine takes parameters as \emph{input}. For example, consider the following (high-level) descriptions of Turing machines $\cal{A}$ and $\cal{B}$:
   177	
   178	\begin{enumerate}
   179		\item Turing machine $\cal{A}$ takes two inputs $(\alpha,x)$ and outputs the integer $\alpha \times x$ where $\alpha, x$ are interpreted as positive integers written in binary. 
   180		\item Turing machine $\cal{B}$ takes one input $x$ and outputs the integer $\beta \times x$ where $\beta$ is a fixed positive integer.
   181	\end{enumerate}
   182	
   183	The description of $\cal{A}$ does not depend on any ``external'' parameters, so its description length $|\desc{\cal{A}}|$ is some universal constant, which we express as $O(1)$. On the other hand, the description of $\cal{B}$ depends on some fixed integer $\beta$; in other words, the parameter $\beta$ is ``hard-wired'' into $\cal{B}$'s description. The description of $\cal{B}$ can be taken to be the following: $\cal{B}$ (which is a $1$-input Turing machine) simulates the execution of the $2$-input Turing machine $\cal{A}$ where the first input tape of $\cal{A}$ has the binary representation of $\beta$ written onto it and the second input tape has $x$ (which is provided as input to $B$) written into it. Thus the description of $\cal{B}$ includes the binary representation of $\beta$, the description of $\cal{A}$ (whose length is a universal constant), and the description of the universal Turing machine (whose length is a universal constant). Thus the description length of $\cal{B}$ is $O(\log \beta) + O(1) = O(\log \beta)$.
   184	
   185	
   186	
   187	\paragraph{Time complexity bounds.} When we bound the time complexity of the Turing machines presented in this paper, we similarly do not worry about the exact
   188	implementation details, but instead we assume that basic computations such as integer arithmetic, string comparisons, etc.\ are all performed
   189	using reasonably efficient algorithms that run in polynomial time in the length of the input. When running other Turing machines as subroutines, we assume that there is some polynomial overhead due to \Cref{thm:universal-tm}.
   190	
   191	
   192	\paragraph{Timeout counters.} We sometimes define Turing machines that are required to halt if 
   193	either the Turing machine or some subroutine takes a number of time steps that exceeds some specified threshold. For example, we may write ``Let $\cal{M}$ be the Turing machine that on input the description $\ol{\cal{R}}$ of a Turing machine $\cal{R}$ and an integer $T$, simulates $\cal{R}$ on the empty tape and halts if more than $T$ steps are performed.''
   194	
   195	This is useful for establishing an \emph{a priori} bound on the time complexity of the Turing machine. In particular we will be able to claim that $\cal{M}$, as described above, always runs in time at most $\poly(T,|\ol{\cal{R}}|$, irrespective of the running time of $\cal{R}$ itself.
   196	
   197	We explain how such a Turing machine can be realized formally. We use a variant of the universal Turing machine of \Cref{thm:universal-tm}. Using the theorem, it is straightforward to show that given a (single tape) Turing machine $\cal{R}$ there exists another two-tape Turing machine $\cal{M}'$ such that, whenever the second tape is initialized to the binary representation of $T$, $\cal{M}'$ simulates $\cal{R}$ and in-between every simulated step of $\cal{R}$, decrements the second tape and checks if it reaches zero. If it does, then $\cal{M}'$ halts and rejects. Otherwise, it continues. 
   198	
   199	The time complexity of $\cal{M}'$ is, by definition, at most $O(T \log T)$ for all inputs. The description length of $\cal{M}'$ is at most $O(|\ol{\cal{R}}|)$, because this is the description size of the universal Turing machine, whose initial tape has been hardwired with $\ol{\cal{R}}$.
   200	To convert back to a single tape Turing machine and obtain $\cal{M}$ from $\cal{M}$' we can use \Cref{thm:universal-tm} again, at the cost of a polynomial blow-up in the time complexity.
   201	
   202	
   203	\paragraph{Input representations.} 
   204	Although the inputs and outputs of a Turing machine are strictly speaking
   205	  binary strings, we oftentimes slightly abuse notation and specify Turing
   206	  machines that treat their inputs and outputs as objects with more structure,
   207	  such as finite field elements, integers, symbols from a larger alphabet, and
   208	  so on.
   209	  In this case we implicitly assume that the Turing machine specification uses a
   210	  consistent convention to represent these structured objects as binary strings.
   211	  Conventions for objects such as integers are straightforward.
   212	  For representations of finite field elements, we refer the reader to
   213	  Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.

   216	\subsection{Linear spaces}
   217	\label{sec:linear-spaces}
   218	
   219	Linear spaces considered in the paper generally take the form $V = \F^n$ for a
   220	finite field $\F$ and integer $n \geq 1$.
   221	In particular, when we write ``let $V$ be a linear space'', unless explicitly
   222	stated otherwise we always mean a space of the form $\F^n$.
   223	Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_2, \ldots, \hat{e}_n\}$ denote the standard basis of $V$, where for
   224	$i \in\{ 1, 2, \ldots, n\}$,
   225	\begin{equation*}
   226	  \hat{e}_i = (0, \ldots, 0, 1, 0, \ldots, 0)
   227	\end{equation*}
   228	has a $1$ in the $i$-th coordinate and $0$'s elsewhere.
   229	We write $\End(V)$ to denote the set of linear transformations from $V$ to
   230	itself.
   231	\begin{definition}[Register subspace]
   232	  A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
   233	  subset of the standard basis of $V$.\footnote{The use of the term ``register''
   234	    is meant to create an analogy for how the space of multiple qubits is often
   235	    partitioned into ``registers'' containing a few qubits each.}
   236	  We often represent such a subspace as an indicator vector $u\in \{0,1\}^s$,
   237	  where $s=\dim(V)$, such that if $\{\hat{e}_1,\ldots,\hat{e}_s\}$ is the standard basis of
   238	  $V$ then $S = \text{span}\{\hat{e}_i|\,u_i=1\}$.
   239	\end{definition}
   240	
   241	\begin{definition}
   242	  Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_i\}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$.
   243	  For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$, $v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V$,
   244	  define the \emph{dot product}
   245	  \begin{equation*}
   246	    u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
   247	  \end{equation*}
   248	  Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. The \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
   249	  \begin{equation*}
   250	    S^\perp \,=\, \big\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0
   251	    \text{ for all }  v \in S \big\}\;.
   252	  \end{equation*}
   253	  Although the notation $S^\perp$ does not explicitly refer to $V$, the ambient
   254	  space will always be clear from context.
   255	\end{definition}
   256	
   257	We note that over finite fields, the notion of orthogonality does not possess
   258	all of the same intuitive properties of orthogonality over fields such as $\R$
   259	or $\C$; for example, a non-zero subspace $S$ may be orthogonal to itself (e.g.\
   260	$\mathrm{span} \{ (1,1) \}$ over $\F_2$).
   261	However, the following remains true over all fields.
   262	
   263	\begin{lemma}
   264	  \label{lem:perp_perp}
   265	  Suppose $S$ is a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) =
   266	  \dim(V)$, and 
   267	  \begin{equation*}
   268	    (S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
   269	  \end{equation*}
   270	\end{lemma}
   271	
   272	\begin{proof}
   273	  The statement about the dimensions follows from the fact that vectors in $S^\perp$ are
   274	  the solution to a feasible linear system of equations with $\dim(S)$ linearly
   275	  independent rows; this implies that the solution space has dimension exactly
   276	  $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$.
   277	  Next, we argue that $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   278	  Let $u \in S$.
   279	  Since all vectors $v \in S^\perp$ are orthogonal to every vector in $S$,
   280	  in particular $u$, this implies that $u \in (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   281	  By dimension counting, it follows that $(S^\perp)^\perp = S$.
   282	\end{proof}
   283	
   284	\begin{definition}\label{def:complementary}
   285	  Given a linear space $V$, two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of $V$ are said to form a
   286	  pair of \emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
   287	\begin{equation*}
   288	  S \cap T = \{ 0 \}, \quad S + T = V\;.
   289	\end{equation*}
   290	In this case, we write $V = S \oplus T$.
   291	Any $x\in V$ can be written as $x = x^S + x^T$ for $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$
   292	in a unique way.
   293	We refer to $x^S$ (resp.~$x^T$) as the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel
   294	  to $T$} (resp.~\emph{onto $T$ parallel to $S$}).
   295	We call the unique linear map $L: V \to V$ that maps $x \mapsto x^S$ the
   296	\emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
   297	\end{definition}
   298	
   299	A given subspace may have many different complementary subspaces: consider the
   300	example of $S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1) \}$ in $\F_2^2$.
   301	Different complementary subspaces include $T = \mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and
   302	$T' = \mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$.
   303	It is convenient to define the notion of a \emph{canonical complement} of a
   304	subspace $S$, given a basis for $S$.
   305	
   306	\begin{definition}
   307	  \label{def:canonical-complement}
   308	  Let $E$ be the standard basis of linear space $V = \F^n$.
   309	  Let $F = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly
   310	  independent vectors in $V$.
   311	  The \emph{canonical complement $F^\perp$ of $F$} is the set of $n-m$ independent
   312	  vectors defined as follows.
   313	  Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i, j}\, \hat{e}_j$.
   314		Using a canonical algorithm for Gaussian elimination that works over arbitrary
   315	  fields, transform the $m\times n$ matrix $(a_{i, j})$ to reduced row echelon
   316	  form $(b_{i, j})$.
   317	  Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices of the leading $1$ entry in each row
   318	  of $(b_{i, j})$.
   319	  The canonical complement is defined as $F^\perp = \{ \hat{e}_j : j \not\in J \}$.
   320	\end{definition}
   321	
   322	
   323	\begin{remark}
   324	We emphasize that the canonical complement $F^\perp$ is a \emph{set} (rather than
   325	a subspace), and it is defined with respect to a \emph{set} of linearly
   326	independent vectors $F$. While there are equivalent ways of defining
   327	a canonical complement of a \emph{subspace} in a basis-independent manner, 
   328	we use this particular definition because it makes it clear that
   329	the canonical complement of a set $F$ is efficiently computable. 
   330	\end{remark}
   331	
   332	\begin{remark}
   333	  Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V$.
   334	  Suppose subspace $S$ is a register subspace of $V$ spanned by
   335	  $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$.
   336	  Then it is not hard to verify that the canonical complement of $\hat{E}_{0}$ is
   337	  $\hat{E}\setminus \hat{E}_0$ and the span of the canonical complement coincides with
   338	  $S^\perp$.
   339	\end{remark}
   340	
   341	
   342	\begin{lemma}
   343	  \label{lem:canonical-complement}
   344	  Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors $F = \{v_1,\ldots,v_m \}
   345	  \subseteq V$ and let $F^\perp$ be the canonical complement of $F$ as defined
   346	  in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   347	  Let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$.
   348	  Then
   349	  \begin{equation*}
   350	   \qquad S + T = V\;,  S \cap T = \{ 0 \} \;.
   351	  \end{equation*}
   352	\end{lemma}
   353	
   354	\begin{proof}
   355	To show the first item, we must show that every vector in $V$ can be
   356	written as a sum of an element of $S$ and an element of $T$. To do
   357	this, let $A = (a_{i, j})$ be the $m\times n$ matrix over $\F$ whose
   358	rows are the vectors $v_i$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   359	  Write $A = U B$ where $U$ is invertible and $B$ is in reduced row echelon
   360	  form.
   361	  Let $J$ be the set of column indices of the leading 1 entries in
   362	  $B$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.  
   363	  Now, the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span the subpsace $S$, and the restriction of
   364	  these rows to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   365	  span $\F^m$. Thus, for any vector $u \in V$, there is some linear
   366	  combination $v$ of rows of $B$ such that $u$ and $v$ agree
   367	  restricted to the columns in $J$. In other words, there exists $v
   368	  \in S$ such that $u_j = v_j$ for all $j \in J$. Hence, $u = v + w$
   369	  for $w \in T$, where $T$ is the canonical complement.
   370	  This shows $S + T = V$.
   371	  Counting dimensions shows that necessarily $S\cap T =
   372	  \{0\}$.
   373	\end{proof}
   374	
   375	\begin{definition}
   376	  \label{def:cl-canonical}
   377	  Let $F \subseteq V$ be a set of linearly independent vectors.
   378	  Let $F^\perp$ be the canonical complement of $F$.
   379	  Define the \emph{canonical linear map $L \in \End(V)$ with kernel basis $F$}
   380	  as the projector onto $T$ parallel to $S$, where $S = \mathrm{span}(F)$ and $T
   381	  = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$.
   382	  When the basis $F$ for $S$ is clear from context, we refer to this map as the
   383	  \emph{canonical linear map with kernel $S$.}
   384	\end{definition}
   385	
   386	\begin{definition}
   387	  \label{def:Lperp}
   388	  Let $L \in \End(V)$ be a linear map, and let $F$ be a basis for
   389	  $\ker(L)^\perp$.
   390	  Define $L^\perp : V \rightarrow V$ as the canonical linear map with kernel
   391	  basis $F$.
   392	\end{definition}
   393	
   394	\begin{lemma}
   395	  \label{lem:L_perp_perp}
   396	  Let $L \in \End(V)$ be a linear map and $F$ a basis for $\ker(L)^\perp$.
   397	  Let $L^\perp \in \End(V)$ be the linear map defined in
   398	  Definition~\ref{def:Lperp}.
   399	  Then $\ker(L^\perp) = \ker(L)^\perp$.
   400	\end{lemma}
   401	
   402	\begin{proof}
   403	  First, to set notation, let $S = \mathrm{span}(F) = \ker(L)^\perp$ and $T =
   404	  \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement},
   405	  any vector $v \in V$ can be uniquely decomposed as $v = v^S +
   406	  v^T$. 
   407	
   408	  Now we will show the lemma.  First we show that if $\ker(L^\perp) \subseteq \ker(L)^\perp$. Let
   409	  $v \in \ker(L^\perp)$, and write $v = v^S + v^T$.  By the definition
   410	  of $L^\perp$, it follows that $v^T = 0$, and hence $v \in S = \ker(L)^\perp$.
   411	
   412	  It remains to show the other direction, that is $\ker(L)^\perp \subseteq
   413	  \ker(L^\perp)$. Let $v \in \ker(L)^\perp = S$. Then $v = v^S + v^T$
   414	  where $v^T = 0$, and hence by the definition of $L^\perp$, $L^\perp
   415	  v = 0$. Hence $v \in \ker(L^\perp)$.
   416	
   417	  
   418	\end{proof}

   420	\subsection{Finite fields}
   421	\label{sec:finite-fields}
   422	
   423	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ be a prime power.
   424	We denote the finite fields of $p$ and $q$ elements by $\Fp$ and $\Fq$
   425	respectively.
   426	The prime $p$ is the characteristic of field $\Fq$, and field $\Fp$ is the
   427	\emph{prime subfield} of $\Fq$.
   428	We sometimes omit the subscript and simply use $\F$ to denote the finite field
   429	when the size of the field is implicit from context.
   430	For general background on finite fields, and explicit algorithms for elementary
   431	arithmetic operations, we refer to~\cite{mullen2013handbook}.
   432	
   433	\subsubsection{Subfields and bases}
   434	\label{sec:subfields}
   435	Let $q$ be a prime power and $k$ an integer. 
   436	The field $\Fq$ is a subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of
   437	dimension $k$ over $\Fq$.
   438	Let $\{ e_i \}_{i=1}^k$ be a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ as a linear space over $\Fq$.
   439	Introduce a bijection $\downsize_q : \F_{q^k} \rightarrow \Fq^k$ between
   440	$\F_{q^k}$ and $\Fq^k$ defined with respect to the basis $\{ e_i \}_{i=1}^k$ by
   441	\begin{equation*}
   442	  \downsize_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k
   443	\end{equation*}
   444	where $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$.
   445	This map satisfies several nice properties.
   446	First, the map is an isomorphism of $\Fq$-vector spaces: it is $\Fq$-linear and addition in $\F_{q^k}$
   447	naturally corresponds to vector addition in $\Fq^k$.
   448	Namely, for all $a,b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   449	\begin{equation*}
   450		\downsize_q (a + b) = \downsize_q(a) + \downsize_q(b)\;.
   451	\end{equation*}
   452	Second, multiplication by a field element in $\F_{q^k}$ corresponds to a linear
   453	map on $\F_{q}^k$.
   454	For all $a \in \F_{q^k}$, there exists a matrix $K_a \in \Matrix_k (\Fq)$ such
   455	that for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   456	\begin{equation*}
   457		\downsize_q (a b) = K_a \, \downsize_q(b)\;.
   458	\end{equation*}
   459	The matrix $K_a$ is called the \emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to
   460	  basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$}.
   461	
   462	We extend the map $\downsize_q$ to vectors, matrices and sets over $\F_{q^k}$.
   463	For $v = (v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$, define
   464	\begin{equation*}
   465	  \downsize_q (v) = \bigl( \downsize_q (v_i) \bigr)_{i=1}^n \in \Fq^{kn}\;.
   466	\end{equation*}
   467	Similarly, for matrix $M = (M_{i, j}) \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$, define
   468	\begin{equation*}
   469	  \downsizem_q (M) = \bigl( K_{M_{i, j}} \bigr) \in \Matrix_{mk, nk} (\Fq)\;,
   470	\end{equation*}
   471	the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th block is the multiplication table $K_{M_{i,
   472	    j}}$ of $M_{i, j}$ with respect to basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$.
   473	For a set $S$ of vectors in $\F_{q^k}^n$, define
   474	\begin{equation*}
   475		\downsize_q(S) = \{ \downsize_q(v) : v \in S \}\;.
   476	\end{equation*}
   477	We omit the subscript and write $\downsize$ and $\downsizem$ for $\downsize_q$
   478	and $\downsizem_q$ respectively when $q$ equals to $p$, the characteristic of
   479	the field.
   480	
   481	The \emph{trace of\/ $\F_{q^k}$ over\/ $\Fq$} is defined as
   482	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   483	  \tr_{q^k \to q} :\; a \,\mapsto \, \Tr(K_a)
   484	\end{equation}
   485	for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $\Tr(K_a)$ is the trace of the multiplication table
   486	of $a$ with respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$.
   487	By definition, the trace is an $\Fq$-linear map from $\F_{q^k}$ to
   488	$\Fq$. The trace is in fact independent of the choice of basis, which
   489	can be seen from the following equivalent definition~\cite[Definition 2.1.80]{mullen2013handbook}:
   490	\[
   491		\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j = 0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   492	\]
   493	
   494	A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', e_2', \ldots, e_k' \}$ of $\{e_1, e_2, \ldots,
   495	e_k\}$ is a basis such that $\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for
   496	all $i, j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$.
   497	A \emph{self-dual basis} is one that is equal to its dual.
   498	If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set $\{ \alpha^{q^j} \}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a
   499	basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\Fq$, the basis is called a \emph{normal
   500	  basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not exist for all fields but are guaranteed to exist under
   501	certain conditions; in particular, if $q = 2$ and $k$ is odd, as will
   502	be shown in \Cref{lem:efficient_basis}.
   503	
   504	We record some convenient facts about the maps $\downsize(\cdot)$ and
   505	$\downsizem(\cdot)$ for self-dual bases.
   506	
   507	\begin{lemma}
   508	  \label{lem:downsize_field}
   509	  Let $q$ be a prime power, $k$ an integer and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual basis for
   510	  $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   511	  The map $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ corresponding to $\{e_i\}$ satisfies the
   512	  following properties:
   513	  \begin{enumerate}
   514	  \item For all $x \in \F_{q^k}$, $\downsize_q(x) = \bigl( \tr_{q^k \to
   515	      q}(xe_1),\ldots,\tr_{q^k \to q}(xe_k) \bigr)$.
   516	  \item For all $x,y \in \F_{q^k}$, $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \downsize_q(x) \cdot
   517	    \downsize_q(y)$.
   518	  \item For all $M \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in
   519	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsizem_q(M) \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(Mv)$.
   520	  \end{enumerate}
   521	\end{lemma}
   522	 
   523	\begin{proof}
   524	  We show each property by direct calculation.
   525	  \begin{enumerate}
   526	    \item Let $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. Then by the definition of
   527	    $\downsize_q$, $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$. Multiplying both sides by $e_j$
   528	    and taking the trace yields $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i
   529	    \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j) = x_j$, where the last equality is by
   530	    self-duality of the basis.
   531	    \item Write $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$ and $\downsize_q(y) =
   532	      (y_1, \dots, y_k)$. Then
   533	      \begin{align*}
   534	        \tr_{q^k \to q} (xy) &= \tr_{q^k \to q}(\sum_{ij} x_i y_j e_i
   535	                               e_j) \\
   536	                             &= \sum_{ij} x_i y_j \tr_{q^k \to q}(  e_i
   537	                               e_j) \\
   538	                             &= \downsize_q(x) \cdot \downsize_q(y),
   539	      \end{align*}
   540	      where the last equality uses the self-duality of the basis.
   541	    \item
   542	      We compute the $i$th $\F_q^k$-block of $\downsize_q(Mv)$:
   543	      \begin{align*}
   544	        \downsize_q(Mv)_i &= \sum_{ij} \downsize_q(M_{ij} v_j) \\
   545	                          &= \sum_{ij} K_{M_{ij}} \downsize_q(v_j) \\
   546	                          &= \downsizem_q(M)_{ij} \downsize_q(v_j) ,
   547	      \end{align*}
   548	      where we have applied the definition of the multiplication table
   549	      $K_{M_{ij}}$ and the map $\downsizem_q(\cdot)$.
   550	  \end{enumerate}
   551	\end{proof}
   552	
   553	For $z\in \F^n$ and $V,W$ a pair of complementary subspaces, recall from
   554	Definition~\ref{def:complementary} the notation $z^V$ for the projection of $z$
   555	onto $V$ and parallel to $W$.
   556	
   557	\begin{lemma}
   558	  \label{lem:downsize_subspace}
   559	  Let $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ denote the map corresponding to a
   560	  basis $\{e_i\}$ for $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   561	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F_{q^k}^n$ with linearly independent basis
   562	  $\{b_1,\ldots,b_t\} \subseteq \F_{q^k}^n$.
   563	  Then the following hold:
   564	  \begin{enumerate}
   565	 	\item $\downsize_q(V)$ is a subspace of $\,\F_{q}^{nk}$.
   566		\item $\{ \downsize_q(e_i b_j) \}_{i,j}$ is a linearly independent basis of
   567	    $\downsize_q(V)$ over $\F_q$.
   568		\item Let $V, W$ be complementary subspaces of $\F_{q^k}^n$.
   569	    Then $V' = \downsize_q(V)$ and $W' = \downsize_q(W)$ are complementary
   570	    subspaces of $\F_q^{kn}$, and furthermore for all vectors $z \in
   571	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsize_q(z^V) = \downsize_q(z)^{V'}$ and
   572	    $\downsize_q(z^W) = \downsize_q(z)^{W'}$.
   573	  \end{enumerate}
   574	\end{lemma}
   575	
   576	\begin{proof}
   577	  For the first item, we first verify that $\downsize_q(V)$ is a subspace.
   578	  Since $V$ is a subspace, it contains $0 \in \F_{q^k}^n$, and therefore $\downsize_q(0)
   579	  = 0$ is also in $\downsize_q(V)$.
   580	  Let $u', v' \in \downsize_q(V)$.
   581	  Using that $\downsize_q$ is a bijection there exist $u,v \in \F_{q^k}^n$ such that
   582	  $u' = \downsize_q(u)$ and $v' = \downsize_q(v)$. Therefore
   583	  \[
   584	    u' + v' = \downsize_q(u) + \downsize_q(v) =
   585	    \downsize_q(u + v) \in \downsize_q(V)\;,
   586	  \]
   587	  where the inclusion follows because $V$ is a subspace and thus contains $u +
   588	  v$.
   589	  Finally, for all $x' \in \F_{q}$, for all $v \in V$, we have that $x'
   590	  \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(x' v)\in \downsize_q(V)$ where we used that $V$
   591	  is closed under scalar multiplication by $\F_{q^k}$ and thus by $\F_q$ (since
   592	  $\F_q$ is a subfield of $\F_{q^k}$).
   593	  Thus $\downsize_q(V)$ is closed under scalar multiplication by $\F_{q}$.
   594	
   595	  For the second item, note that an element $v \in V$ can be expressed uniquely
   596	  as $v = \sum_{i = 1}^t v_i b_i$ for $v_i \in \F_{q^k}$.
   597	  The element $v_i$ can further be written as $\sum_j v_{i, j} e_j$ where $v_{i,
   598	    j} \in \F_q$.
   599	  Thus $v$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\{ e_j b_i \}$, and therefore
   600	  $\downsize_q(v)$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\{ \downsize_q (e_j
   601	  b_i) \}$.
   602	  To establish that the vectors $\{ \downsize_q(e_j b_i) \}$ are linearly
   603	  independent, suppose towards contradiction that they are not.
   604	  Then there would exist $\alpha_{i, j} \in \F_q$ such that at least one
   605	  $\alpha_{i, j}$ is nonzero and
   606	  \begin{align*}
   607	    0 & = \sum_{i,j} \alpha_{i, j} \downsize_q(e_j b_i) \\
   608	      & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \bigl (\sum_j \alpha_{i, j}
   609	        e_j \bigr) b_i \Bigr) \\
   610	      & = \downsize_q \left ( \sum_i \beta_i b_i \right ),
   611	  \end{align*}
   612	  where we define $\beta_i = \sum_j \alpha_{i, j} e_j$.
   613	  Since at least one $\alpha_{i, j} \neq 0$ and the $\{e_j\}$ are linearly
   614	  independent over $\F_q$, there exists $i$ such that $\beta_i \neq 0$, which
   615	  means that there is a non-trivial linear combination of the basis elements
   616	  $b_i$ that equals $0$ under $\downsize_q(\cdot)$.
   617	  Since $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is injective, we get a contradiction with linear
   618	  independence of the $\{b_i\}$.
   619	
   620	  For the third item, we observe that $\downsize_q(V)$ and $\downsize_q(W)$ must
   621	  be complementary because $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is a linear map as well as a
   622	  bijection.
   623	  Let $\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}$ and $\{v_{m+1},\ldots,v_n\}$ denote bases for $V$ and
   624	  $W$, respectively.
   625	  Thus the set $\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}$ forms a basis for $\F_{q^k}^n$, and from the
   626	  previous item, the set $\{ \downsize_q(e_j v_i) \}_{i,\, j}$ is a basis for
   627	  $\F_q^{kn}$.
   628	  Furthermore, the sets $\{ \downsize_q(e_j v_i) \}_{j,\,i = 1,\ldots m}$ and
   629	  $\{ \downsize_q(e_j v_i) \}_{j,\, i = m+1,\ldots n}$ are bases for
   630	  $\downsize_q(V)$ and $\downsize_q(W)$, respectively.
   631	
   632	  There is a unique choice of coefficients $\alpha_{i, j} \in \F_q$ such that
   633	  $\downsize_q(z) = \sum_{i, j} \alpha_{i, j} \downsize_q(e_j v_i)$.
   634	  But then
   635	  \begin{align*}
   636	    \downsize_q(z) & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \bigl ( \sum_j
   637	                     \alpha_{i, j} e_j \bigr) v_i \Bigr) \\
   638	                   & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \alpha_i v_i \Bigr)\;,
   639	  \end{align*}
   640	  where we define $\alpha_i = \sum_j \alpha_{i, j} e_j$.
   641	  Since $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is a bijection, this implies that $z = \sum_i
   642	  \alpha_i v_i$, and therefore $z^V = \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i v_i$ (and similarly
   643	  $z^W = \sum_{i=m+1}^n \alpha_i v_i$).
   644	  This implies that
   645	  \begin{equation*}
   646		  \downsize_q(z)^{V'} = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j} \alpha_{i, j}
   647	    \downsize_q(e_j v_i) = \downsize_q (z^V)\;,
   648	  \end{equation*}
   649	  and similarly $\downsize_q(z)^{W'} = \downsize_q(z^W)$.
   650	  This completes the proof of the lemma.
   651	\end{proof}

   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}
   727	
   728	For $q=2^k$ for $k$ odd (i.e.\ $q$ is an admissible field size) we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q\to 2}$.
   729	
   730	\begin{lemma}
   731	  \label{lem:one}
   732	  Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ be a self-dual normal basis of
   733	  $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   734	  Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and furthermore the representation
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   736	  $\F_2^k$.
   737	\end{lemma}
   738	
   739	\begin{proof}
   740	  Since $\{e_i \}$ is a normal basis, $e_i = \alpha^{2^i}$ for some element
   741	  $\alpha \in \F_{2^k}$.
   742	  Furthermore, for every element $b \in \F_{2^k}$, we have that $\tr(b^2) =
   743	  \tr(b)$.
   744	  This is because
   745	  \[
   746	    \tr(b^2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b^{2^{i+1}} =
   747	    \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1} b^{2^i} = \tr(b)\;,
   748	  \]
   749	  where we use that $b^{2^k} = b$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   750	  Since $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$, we get that $\tr(e_i) = \tr(e_j)$ for all $i,j$.
   751	  It cannot be the case that $\tr(e_i) = 0$ for all $i$.
   752	  Suppose that this were the case.
   753	  This would imply that $\tr(b) = 0$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   754	  But then for all $j \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$ and for some $b \neq 0$, we would
   755	  also have by item 1 of \Cref{lem:downsize_field} that $b_j = \tr(b e_j) = 0$ where $b = \sum_j b_j e_j$ with $b_j \in
   756	  \F_2$.
   757	  This implies that $b$ is the all zero element of $\F_{2^k}$, which is a
   758	  contradiction.
   759	  Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i=1, 2, \ldots, k$.
   760	
   761		The ``furthermore'' part follows item 1 of
   762	        \Cref{lem:downsize_field}:
   763	        \begin{equation*}
   764	          \downsize(1) = (\tr(1 \cdot e_1), \dots, \tr(1 \cdot e_k))
   765	          = (1, \dots, 1).
   766	        \end{equation*}
   767	\end{proof}
   768	
   769	\begin{lemma}
   770	  \label{lem:efficient_arithmetic}
   771	  For any odd integer $k$, let $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ denote the self-dual normal basis
   772	  of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ that is returned by the algorithm specified in
   773	  Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_basis} on input $k$.
   774	  Then the following can be computed in time $\poly(k)$ on input $k$:
   775	  \begin{enumerate}
   776	  \item The representation $\downsize(a+b)$ of the sum $a+b$ given the
   777	    representations $\downsize(a)$ and $\downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   778		\item The representation $\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ given the
   779	    representations $\downsize(a)$ and $\downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   780	  \item The multiplication table $K_a \in \Matrix_k(\F_2)$ given the
   781	    representation $\downsize(a)$ of  $a\in \F_{2^k}$.
   782	  \item The representation $\downsize(a^{-1})$ of the multiplicative inverse of
   783	    $a \in \F_{2^k}$, given the representation $\downsize(a)$.
   784		\item The trace $\tr(a)$ given the multiplication table $K_a$ of $a \in \F_{2^k}$.
   785	  \end{enumerate}
   786	  Furthermore, for all integers $n$, the representations of projections
   787	  $\downsize(x^S)$ and $\downsize(x^T)$ of $x \in \F_{2^k}^n$ for complementary
   788	  subspaces $S,T$ of $\F_{2^k}^n$ can be computed in $\poly(k,n)$ time, given
   789	  the representations $\downsize(x)$, $\{\downsize(v_1), \downsize(v_2), \ldots,
   790	  \downsize(v_m)\}$ and $\{\downsize(w_1), \downsize(w_2), \ldots,
   791	  \downsize(w_{n - m})\}$ where $\{v_i\}$ and $\{w_j\}$ are bases for $S$ and
   792	  $T$ respectively.
   793	\end{lemma}
   794	
   795	\begin{proof}
   796	  Given an odd integer $k$ as input, by Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_basis} it is
   797	  possible to compute the self-dual normal basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ together with the
   798	  multiplication tables $K_{e_i}$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, k$.
   799	  Addition is performed component-wise, and multiplication is done
   800	  using Eq.~\eqref{eq:eq-mult}.
   801	  For the multiplication table $K_a$ it suffices to compute the $k$ products
   802	  $\downsize(a e_i)$ for $i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$.
   803	  To compute inverses, observe that $\downsize(1) = \downsize(aa^{-1}) = K_a
   804	  \downsize(a^{-1})$.
   805	  The matrices $K_a$ are invertible over $\F_2$, so therefore $\downsize(a^{-1}) =
   806	  K_a^{-1} \downsize(1)$; moreover, $\kappa(1)$ is the all-ones vector
   807	  by Lemma~\ref{lem:one} and can thus be efficiently computed.
   808	  Inverting the matrix can be done in $\poly(k)$ time via Gaussian elimination.
   809	  The trace of an element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is by definition the trace of the
   810	  multiplication table $K_a$.
   811	
   812	  For the ``Furthermore'' part, we observe that since $\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m
   813	  \} \cup \{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_{n-m} \}$ forms a basis for $\F_{2^k}^n$, there
   814	  is a unique way to write $x$ as a $\F_{2^k}$ linear combination of $\{ v_i\}$
   815	  and $\{w_j\}$.
   816	  Via Gaussian elimination over $\F_{2^k}$, the $\F_2$-representation of the
   817	  coefficients of this linear combination can be computed in $\poly(n,k)$ time.
   818	  Here we use that addition, multiplication and division over $\F_{2^k}$ can be
   819	  performed in time $\poly(k)$ using the previous items of the Lemma.
   820	\end{proof}
   821	
   822	\begin{remark}
   823	  \label{rmk:tm_fields}
   824	  Throughout this paper, whenever we refer to Turing machines that perform
   825	  computations with elements of a field $\F_q$ for an admissible field size $q =
   826	  2^k$, we mean that that the Turing machines are representing elements of
   827	  $\F_q$ as vectors in $\{0,1\}^{k}$ using the basis specified by the
   828	  algorithm of Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_basis} and performing arithmetic as
   829	  described in Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}.
   830	\end{remark}

   832	\subsection{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   833	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   834	
   835	In this section, we introduce some basic definitions about polynomials over finite fields. 
   836	An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   837	\[
   838		f(x_1,\ldots,x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^m} c_\alpha
   839	  x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   840	\]
   841	where $\{c_\alpha\}$ is a collection of coefficients in $\F_q$.
   842	We say that $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if
   843	$\alpha_i \leq d $ for all $1\leq i\leq m$, and that it has \emph{total degree
   844	  (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if $\sum_i \alpha_i \leq d$.
   845	(Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are polynomials with individual degree
   846	$1$.
   847	
   848	Low-degree polynomials play an important role in this paper.
   849	For one, the classical and quantum low-degree tests of \Cref{sec:ldt} are
   850	nonlocal games that efficiently certify that the players' answers are consistent
   851	with low-degree polynomials.
   852	Low-degree polynomials are also crucial in the probabilistically checkable
   853	proofs (PCP) construction that are used in ``answer reduction'' transformation
   854	(\Cref{sec:ans}).
   855	
   856	We recall the Schwartz-Zippel lemma: 
   857	
   858	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz-Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]
   859	  \label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   860	  Let $f, g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials with total degree at most $d$. Then
   861	  \begin{equation*}
   862	    \Pr_{x \sim \F_q^m}[f(x) = g(x)] \leq d/q\;.
   863	  \end{equation*}
   864	\end{lemma}
   865	
   866	
   867	\paragraph{The low-degree code.}
   868	The Schwartz-Zippel lemma implies that the set of low-degree polynomials form an
   869	error-correcting code with good distance, which we call the \emph{low-degree
   870	  code}.\footnote{It is also known as the \emph{generalized Reed-Muller code} in
   871	  the coding theory literature.}
   872	
   873	Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$.
   874	For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ define the following $m$-variate multilinear
   875	polynomial over $\F_q$:
   876	\[
   877		\ind_{m,y}(x) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i: y_i = 0} (1 - x_i) \;.
   878	\]
   879	Here, we identify $\{0,1\}$ as a subset of $\F_q$.
   880	Notice that, when restricted to the subcube $\{0,1\}^m$, $\ind_{m, y}$ is zero
   881	everywhere except for when $x = y$.
   882	For $a\in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y\in \{0,1\}^m$
   883	(identifying the latter set with $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ using, say, the lexicographic
   884	ordering on strings).
   885	For any such $a$ define the multilinear polynomial $g_a: \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   886	called the \emph{low-degree encoding of $a$}, as follows:
   887	\begin{equation}
   888	\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   889		 g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)\;.
   890	\end{equation}
   891	Note that for any $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_a(y) = a_y$.
   892	Furthermore, the map $a\mapsto g_a$ is linear: for every $x \in \F_q^m$,
   893	\begin{equation}
   894	\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   895		g_a(x) = a \cdot \ind_m(x)\;,
   896	\end{equation}
   897	where $\ind_m(x)$ is the vector $(\ind_{m,y}(x))_{y \in \{0,1\}^m}\in\F_q^M$.
   898	
   899	\begin{lemma}
   900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.
   909	  Via \Cref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}, evaluating $\ind_{m,y}(x)$ takes time
   910	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ because it requires performing $m$ multiplications of $\F_q$
   911	  elements, and therefore the product $a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)$ requires
   912	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ time.
   913	  Computing the sum over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ requires $M \cdot \poly(m,\log q)
   914	  = \poly(M,\log q)$ time, as claimed.
   915	\end{proof}
   916	
   917	Finally, for any $H \subseteq \F_q$ we define the \emph{decoding} map
   918	$\coded_H(\cdot)$ which takes as input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and
   919	returns the following vector $a \in \F_q^M$: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, if $g(y)
   920	\in H$, then set $a_y = g(y)$, and otherwise set $a_y = 0$.
   921	Note that for all $a \in H^M$ we have $\coded_H(g_a) = a$ where $g_a$ is the
   922	low-degree encoding of $a$.
   923	For notational brevity we often write $\coded(\cdot)$ to denote the boolean
   924	decoding map $\coded_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.

   927	\label{sec:lin-reg}
   928	
   929	For a set $V$, we write $\C^V$ for the complex vector space of dimension $|V|$.
   930	The space $\C^V$ is endowed with a canonical orthonormal basis
   931	$\{\ket{x}\}_{x\in V}$.
   932	By ``a quantum state on $V$'' we mean a unit vector
   933	\begin{equation*}
   934	  \ket{\psi}_V \in \complex^V\;.
   935	\end{equation*}
   936	If $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k V_k$ is the direct sum of subspaces $V_k$ over $\F$,
   937	then $\complex^V$ can be identified with $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k
   938	\complex^{V_i}$, by the identification of $\ket{x_1 \oplus \dots \oplus
   939	  x_k}$ with $\ket{x_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \ket{x_k}$.
   940	As a special case, if $\{e_i\}$ is a basis of $V$ the decomposition $V =
   941	\bigoplus_{i=1}^k ( \F e_i)$ yields the tensor product decomposition $\C^V =
   942	\bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{\abs{\F}}$.
   943	We sometimes refer to the spaces $\C^{\abs{\F}}$ as the ``qudits'' of $\C^V$ (or
   944	of a state on it).
   945	
   946	\begin{definition}
   947	  \label{def:EPR}
   948	  For a linear space $V$ over a finite field $\F$, define the \EPR state on $\C^V
   949	  \otimes \C^V$ by
   950	  \begin{equation*}
   951	    \ket{\EPR}_V = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\abs{V}}} \sum_{x\in V}\ket {x}\otimes \ket{x}\;.
   952	  \end{equation*}
   953	  We also write $\ket{\EPR}_{\F_q}$ as $\ket{\EPR_q}$ and $\ket{\EPR_2}$ as
   954	  $\ket{\EPR}$.
   955	\end{definition}

   957	\subsection{Measurements and observables}
   958	
   959	Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued
   960	measures (POVMs).
   961	A POVM consists of a set of positive semidefinite operators $\{ M_a \}_{a\in S}$
   962	indexed by outcomes $a\in S$ that satisfy the condition $\sum_a M_a = I$. If the latter condition is relaxed to $\sum_a M_a \leq I$ then we refer to $\{M_a\}$ as a \emph{sub-measurement}.
   963	We sometimes use the same letter $M$ to refer to the collection of operators
   964	defining the POVM.
   965	The probability that the measurement returns outcome $a$ on state $\ket{\psi}$
   966	is given by
   967	\begin{equation*}
   968	  \Pr(a) = \bra{\psi} M_a \ket{\psi}\;.
   969	\end{equation*}
   970	A POVM $M=\{M_a\}$ is said to be \emph{projective} if each operator $M_a$ is a
   971	projector ($M_a^2 = M_a$). This automatically implies that operators
   972	$M_a, M_b$ for distinct outcomes $a \neq b$ are orthogonal ($M_a M_b =
   973	M_b M_a = 0$). An \emph{observable} is a unitary matrix.
   974	A \emph{binary observable} is an observable $O$ such that $O^2 = \Id$, i.e.\ $O$
   975	has eigenvalues in $\{-1,1\}$.
   976	
   977	We follow the convention that subscripts of the measurement index
   978	the outcome and superscripts of the measurement are used to index different
   979	measurements.
   980	For example, we use $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$ to represent a measurement indexed by $x$
   981	whose outcome consists of two parts $a$ and $b$.
   982	In this case, by slightly abusing the notation, we use $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$
   983	to denote
   984	\begin{equation*}
   985	  M^x_a = \sum_b M^x_{a,\, b}\;, \quad M^x_b = \sum_a M^x_{a,\, b}\;.
   986	\end{equation*}
   987	For any $x$, $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$ are POVMs sometimes referred to as the
   988	``marginals'' of $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$.
   989	
   990	\begin{definition}
   991	  \label{def:bracket}
   992	  Let $\{M^x_a\}_{a\in A}$ be a family of POVMs indexed by $x\in \cal{X}$.
   993	  Let $f:A\to B$ be an arbitrary function.
   994	  We write $\bigl\{ M^x_{[f(\cdot)=b]} \bigr\}$ for the POVM derived from
   995	  $\{M^x_a\}$ by applying the function $f$ before returning the outcome.
   996	  More precisely,
   997	\begin{equation*}
   998	  M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]} = \sum_{a : f(a)=b} M^x_a\;.
   999	\end{equation*}
  1000	If $b$ is not in the image of $f$, then we define $M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]}$ to be
  1001	$0$. In cases where the outcome $a$ has a natural interpretation as a tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$ we sometimes slightly abuse notation and write $M^x_{[a_i=b]}$ for some $i\in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ to denote 
  1002	\[ M^x_{[a_i=b]} \,=\,\sum_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k):\,a_i=b} M^x_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k)}\;.\]
  1003	\end{definition}

  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform
  1105	\begin{equation}
  1106	  \label{eq:fourier-f}
  1107	  F \,=\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b\in \Fq} \omega^{-\tr(ab)}
  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.
  1109	\end{equation}
  1110	Explicitly, the eigenbases consist of the vectors $\ket{e_W}$ labeled by an
  1111	element $e \in \Fq$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
  1112	\begin{equation*}
  1113	  \ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_j \omega^{- \tr(e j)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
  1114	  \ket{e_Z}   = \ket{e}\;.
  1115	\end{equation*}
  1116	We denote the POVM whose elements are projectors onto basis vectors of the
  1117	eigenbasis associated with the observables $\qp^W$ by $\{\qp^W_e\}_e$.
  1118	Then for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a\in \Fq$, the observables $\qp^W(a)$ can be
  1119	written as
  1120	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1121	  \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(a b)} \qp^W_b\;.
  1122	\end{equation}
  1123	
  1124	To invert this relation, we first quote the following useful Fourier fact.
  1125	\begin{lemma}[Fact 3.2 of \cite{NW19}]
  1126	  \label{lem:cancellation}
  1127	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F^k$. For all $v \not\in V^\perp$, 
  1128	  \begin{equation*}
  1129	    \E_{u \sim V} \omega^{\tr(u \cdot v)} = 0\;,
  1130	  \end{equation*}
  1131	  where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $u$ from $V$.
  1132	\end{lemma}
  1133	
  1134	We may now invert~\Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}:
  1135	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single}
  1136	  \E_{a\in \F_q} \omega^{-\tr(ab)} \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b'\in \F_q} \E_{a\in \F_q}
  1137	  \omega^{\tr(a(b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;,
  1138	\end{equation}
  1139	where the second step follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation}.
  1140	
  1141	For systems with many qudits, we will consider tensor products of the operators
  1142	$\qp^W$.
  1143	Slightly abusing notation, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$ and $a \in \Fq^n$ we denote by
  1144	$\qp^W(a)$ the tensor product $\qp^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \qp^W(a_n)$.
  1145	These obey the twisted commutation relations
  1146	\begin{equation*}
  1147	  \forall a,b\in \Fq^n,\qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) \,=\, \omega^{-\tr (a \cdot
  1148	    b)}\, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;,
  1149	\end{equation*}
  1150	where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i \in \Fq$.
  1151	For $W\in\{X,Z\}$ and $e \in \Fq^n$ define the eigenstates
  1152	\[ \ket{e_W} = \ket{(e_1)_W} \ot \dots \ot \ket{(e_n)_W}\;, \]
  1153	and associated rank-$1$ projectors $\qp^W_e$. Analogous versions of \Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1154	and \Cref{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single} relate the multi-qubit observables
  1155	and projectors:
  1156	\begin{align}
  1157	  \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b \in \Fq^n} \omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}
  1158	  \qp^W_b\;, \label{eq:pauli-obs-proj} \\
  1159	    \E_{a\in \F_q^n} \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)} \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b'\in \F_q^n} \E_{a\in \F_q^n}
  1160	  \omega^{\tr(a\cdot (b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;. \label{eq:pauli-inversion-0}
  1161	\end{align}
  1162	
  1163	Since we only consider finite fields $\F_q$ such that $q = 2^k$ the maximally
  1164	entangled state $\ket{\EPR_q}$ and the corresponding qudit Pauli
  1165	observables/projectors are isomorphic to a tensor product of maximally entangled
  1166	states $\ket{\EPR_2}$ and \emph{qubit} Pauli observables/projectors
  1167	respectively; this is shown in the next lemma.
  1168	This is used to argue that the Pauli basis test (described in
  1169	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) gives a self-test for Pauli observables and
  1170	maximally entangled states over qubits.
  1171	
  1172	\begin{lemma}
  1173	  \label{lem:pauli-binary}
  1174	  For all admissible field sizes $q = 2^k$ and integers $L$, there exists
  1175	  an isomorphism $\phi: (\C^q)^{\otimes L} \to (\C^2)^{\otimes L k}$
  1176	  such that\footnote{ Here we have applied the natural identifications between
  1177	  $(\C^q)^{\ot L} \ot (\C^q)^{\ot L}$ and $(\C^q \ot \C^q)^{\ot L}$,
  1178	  and between $(\C^2)^{\ot L k} \ot (C^2)^{\ot Lk}$ and $(\C^2 \ot
  1179	  \C^2)^{\ot Lk}$.}
  1180	\begin{equation}
  1181	    \label{eq:epr-q-to-epr-2}
  1182	    \phi \otimes \phi \, \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes L} =
  1183	    \ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes L k}\;.
  1184	  \end{equation}
  1185	  Moreover, for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and for all $u \in \F_q^L$
  1186		\begin{equation}
  1187		\label{eq:pauli-q-to-pauli-2}
  1188	  	\tau^W_u = \phi^\dagger\, \Bigl (\bigotimes_{i=1}^L
  1189	    \bigotimes_{j=1}^{k} \sigma^{W}_{u_{ij}} \Bigr) \, \phi\;.
  1190		\end{equation}
  1191		Here, the $(u_{ij})_{i,j}$ denotes a vector of $\F_2$ values such that $u_i =
  1192	  \sum_j u_{ij} e_j$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots,L\}$ with
  1193	  $\{e_1,\ldots,e_{k}\}$ being the self-dual normal basis of $\F_q$ over $\F_2$
  1194	  specified by Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_basis}.
  1195	  For $i\in\{1,\ldots,L\}$ and $j\in\{1,\ldots,q\}$ the $(i,j)$-th factor
  1196	  $\sigma^{W}_{u_{ij}}$ denotes the projector $\frac{1}{2} \left ( \Id +
  1197	    (-1)^{u_{ij}} \sigma^W(1) \right)$ acting on the $s$-th qubit of
  1198	  $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes L k}$, where $s = (i-1) k + j$.
  1199	\end{lemma}
  1200	
  1201	\begin{proof}
  1202	Define the isometry $\theta : \C^q \to (\C^2)^{\otimes k}$ as $\theta\,
  1203	  \ket{a} = \ket{a_1} \otimes \ket{ a_2} \cdots \ket{a_k}$ where $\kappa(a) = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k)
  1204	  \in \F_2^k$ is the bijection introduced in Section~\ref{sec:finite-fields}
  1205	  corresponding to the basis $\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\}$. Observe that
  1206	  $\theta \otimes \theta \ket{\EPR_{2^k}} = \ket{\EPR_2}^{\ot k}$.
  1207	
  1208	  Let $a \in \F_q$, and let $\kappa(a) = (a_1,\ldots,a_k) \in \F_2^k$.
  1209	  Then from~\eqref{eq:pauli-inversion-0}, we get
  1210	  \begin{equation}
  1211	    \label{eq:qudit-to-qubit-pauli-1}
  1212	    \begin{split}
  1213	      \tau^W_a
  1214	      & = \E_{b \in \F_q} (-1)^{\tr(a b)} \, \tau^W(b) \\
  1215	      & = \E_{b \in \F_q} (-1)^{\tr(\sum_j a_j e_j b)} \, \tau^W(b) \\
  1216	      & = \E_{b \in \F_q} (-1)^{\sum_j a_j b_j} \,
  1217	      \tau^W \left ( \sum_j b_j e_j \right) \;,
  1218	    \end{split}

\begin{definition}[Consistency between POVMs]\label{def:consistency}
	\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.consistencyDefect, MIPStarRE.QPBT.IsConsistentWithin}
	\leanok
	\uses{def:povm-conventions, def:state-distance}
	Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mathcal X$. Let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ be a quantum state, and for all $x \in \mathcal X$ let $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ be POVMs. We write
	\[
		A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a
	\]
	on state $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ if
	\[
		\E_{x \sim \mu} \sum_{a \ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^x_b \ket{\psi} = O(\delta)\,.
	\]
	In this case we say that $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are \emph{$\delta$-consistent} on $\ket{\psi}$. As in Definition~\ref{def:state-distance}, the $O(\cdot)$ refers to families of POVMs and states indexed by an implicit parameter $n \in \N$, and is taken as $n \to \infty$.
\end{definition}

A measurement that is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement} is $0$-consistent with itself on the same state under the singleton distribution, and vice versa: if $\sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \ot M_a \ket{\psi} = 1$, then $M_a \ot \Id\, \ket{\psi} = \Id \ot M_a\, \ket{\psi}$ for every $a$, by the equality case of the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality applied outcome by outcome.

/-! # Polynomial error predicates

Shared quantitative predicates for the polynomial-error bounds in QPBT
chapters 12, 14, and 15.

## References

These are formalization-only auxiliaries for polynomially small QPBT error
functions. The one-parameter form includes the explicit square-root witnesses
in paper chapter 14; the two-parameter form is used by `lem:pasting` in paper
chapter 6.
-/

namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT

open scoped BigOperators

/-- The literal finite-arity polynomial bound of
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:26-29`, retained as an **unasserted**
predicate. One positive constant is both prefactor and exponent, uniformly over
all strictly positive inputs. The source shorthand imposes neither a value at
zero nor an additional lower bound on the function.

This is not `IsPolyErr` or `IsPolyErr₂` and no implication from those corrected
predicates is asserted. See `docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_polynomial-error-square-root.tex`
and `docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_pasting-product-error.tex`, issues #16, #196, and #674. -/
def PrintedPolynomialBound {k : ℕ} (f : (Fin k → ℝ) → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ x : Fin k → ℝ, (∀ i, 0 < x i) →
    f x ≤ C * Real.rpow (∏ i, x i) C

/-- The square-root choice under the literal polynomial convention, retained
**without being asserted**. Paper `lem:qld-comm-cons` and
`lem:qld-comm-line-cons` choose `sqrt ε` in
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:508-520,649-676`.
This proposition records only their scalar contract, not their operator
conclusions. It is refuted by the elementary calculation in
`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_polynomial-error-square-root.tex`, issue #16: the input
one forces `C ≥ 1`, after which small positive inputs contradict the bound.
Defining this proposition is not a proof of it. -/
def PrintedSquareRootPolynomialClaim : Prop :=
  PrintedPolynomialBound (fun x : Fin 1 → ℝ => Real.sqrt (x 0))

/-- A nonnegative one-parameter error function bounded by a positive real power.

**Local fix:** The prefactor and exponent are quantified separately. Paper
chapter 14 explicitly obtains `sqrt ε` at
`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:508-520,649-676`, which the coupled
constant in the shorthand at `04_preliminaries.tex:26-29` cannot bound on all
positive inputs. The correction is documented in
`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_polynomial-error-square-root.tex` and tracked by issue
#16. -/
def IsPolyErr (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ C r : ℝ, 1 ≤ C ∧ 0 < r ∧ ∀ x, 0 ≤ x →
    0 ≤ f x ∧ f x ≤ C * Real.rpow x r

/-- A nonnegative two-parameter error function bounded by a sum of positive
real powers.

**Local fix:** The prefactor and the two exponents are quantified separately,
and the bound is imposed on the closed nonnegative quadrant. The shorthand at
`04_preliminaries.tex:22-29` reads `poly` of several arguments as a single
power of their product, which forces the pasting error of `lem:pasting` at
`06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:504-525` to tend to zero with the collision
error at every fixed positive consistency error; a two-dimensional strategy
refutes the resulting statement. A sum of separate positive powers vanishes
exactly when both errors vanish, and bounds the terms the imported proof of
Fact 4.35 produces. The correction is documented in
`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_pasting-product-error.tex` and tracked by issue #196. -/
def IsPolyErr₂ (f : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ C r s : ℝ, 1 ≤ C ∧ 0 < r ∧ 0 < s ∧ ∀ x y, 0 ≤ x → 0 ≤ y →
    0 ≤ f x y ∧ f x y ≤ C * (Real.rpow x r + Real.rpow y s)

end MIPStarRE.QPBT

\section{At a glance}

\begin{itemize}

\section{Key theorem forms}

The source asks for an error function
$\delta_{\mathrm{pasting}}(\eta,\delta)$ satisfying
\[
  \delta_{\mathrm{pasting}}(\eta,\delta)
    = \operatorname{poly}(\eta,\delta)
\]
and bounding the final consistency defect whenever the three input defects are
at most $\delta$ and the codeword-collision probability is at most $\eta$.
Under the paper's global convention, the displayed polynomial assertion means
that there is a universal $C>0$ such that
\[
  \delta_{\mathrm{pasting}}(\eta,\delta) \leq C(\eta\delta)^C
  \qquad (\eta,\delta>0).
  \tag{product contract}
\]
The imported proof instead accumulates terms depending separately on the two
errors, including $O(\delta^{1/2})$, $O((\delta+\eta)^{1/2})$, and $\eta$.
A compatible corrected theorem form would use, for example, an upper bound by
$A(\eta^r+\delta^s)$ for universal $A\geq1$ and $r,s>0$.
The polynomial shorthand itself is only an upper bound on positive inputs;
it supplies neither axis values nor an additional nonnegativity condition.
The corrected predicate supplies both on the closed nonnegative quadrant.

\section{The source assertion}

Lemma~\texttt{lem:pasting} of \cite[lines~504--525]{Ji2020MIPStar} imports
Fact~4.35 from the NEEXP paper.  Its error is declared to be
$\operatorname{poly}(\eta,\delta)$.  The asymptotic convention in
\cite[lines~19--29]{Ji2020MIPStar} requires every variable to occur in the
product on the right side of the product contract.  The proof of the imported
fact, however, bounds the two sources of error independently; see
\cite[lines~1030--1209]{Natarajan2018NEEXP}.%
\footnote{The mirrored passages are
\path{references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex}, lines~19--29;
\path{references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex}, lines~504--525;
and \path{references/neexp-paper/05_quantum_preliminaries.tex},
lines~1030--1209.}

More explicitly, fix a probability distribution $\mathcal D$ on
$(x,y_1,y_2)$, a unit bipartite state $\psi$, and nonnegative $\eta,\delta$.
Let $G_i^x$ be measurements indexed by functions
$g_i:\mathcal Y_i\to\mathcal R_i$, with $G_2^x$ projective, and let
$A^{x,y_1,y_2}$ be a projective joint answer measurement. Assume that distinct
second codewords agree with conditional probability at most $\eta$, given
$(x,y_1)$ whenever this conditioning has positive probability. Write
$Q_{i,a_i}=(G_i)^x_{[\operatorname{eval}_{y_i}(\cdot)=a_i]}$.
The input comparisons, averaged over $\mathcal D$, are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pasting-1}
 A^{x,y_1,y_2}_{a_i}\ot\mathrm{Id}
 \simeq_\delta\mathrm{Id}\ot Q_{i,a_i}\quad(i=1,2),
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pasting-2}
 A^{x,y_1,y_2}_{a_1,a_2}\ot\mathrm{Id}
 \simeq_\delta\mathrm{Id}\ot A^{x,y_1,y_2}_{a_1,a_2}.
\end{equation}
Define $J^x_{g_1,g_2}=(G_2)^x_{g_2}(G_1)^x_{g_1}(G_2)^x_{g_2}$.
The asserted universal function $\delta_{\mathrm{pasting}}$ bounds
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pasting-3}
 A^{x,y_1,y_2}_{a_1,a_2}\ot\mathrm{Id}
 \simeq_{\delta_{\mathrm{pasting}}(\eta,\delta)}
 \mathrm{Id}\ot J^x_{[g_1(y_1)=a_1,\,g_2(y_2)=a_2]}.
\end{equation}

state, and measurements. There is a second constant convention to distinguish:
\texttt{def:consistency}, chapter 6 lines 233--250, defines
$\simeq_\delta$ using $O(\delta)$, not an exact bound by $\delta$.
Writing $c_{\rm in}>0$ for a common upper bound on the three input
constants, the output constant $c_{\rm out}>0$ may depend on
$c_{\rm in}$ but must be uniform in the errors and measurement data.
It cannot be silently absorbed into a coupled prefactor and exponent.

The full finite-dimensional assertion is now retained as the unasserted
\leanid{PrintedPastingClaim} in
\doclink{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Games/Sandwich.lean}. It chooses the error function
with \leanid{PrintedPolynomialBound} before the constants and all data,

The codeword collections are finite sets of actual functions, rather than
arbitrary labels whose evaluation maps might identify distinct codewords.
Finite-type and decidability instances implement finite sums; normalization
and probability mass are explicit. The shared local matrix space permits
the same answer measurement on the two registers, without assuming symmetry
of the state. No assertion for infinite-dimensional families is encoded.
The well-formed conditional law excludes zero-mass fibers, as in the
existing collision API. The bound on the error function concerns strictly
positive inputs, while the three comparisons are retained for nonnegative
errors. This definition is not a theorem, a new proof assumption, or a
proof of the product contract.

\section{A two-dimensional counterexample}

Fix $0<\rho<1$.  Let every question set, both codeword sets, and the second
answer set be a singleton, and let the first answer set be $\{0,1\}$.  Use the
point-mass question distribution and local Hilbert spaces $\C^2$.  In the
standard basis, take the normalized bipartite state
\[
  \ket{\psi_\rho}
    = \sqrt{1-\rho}\ket{0,0}+\sqrt{\rho}\ket{1,1}.
\]
Let both codeword measurements have their sole effect equal to the identity,
and evaluate the sole first codeword to $0$.  Let the joint answer measurement
be the standard-basis projective measurement: its effects at $(0,*)$ and
$(1,*)$ are respectively $\ket{0}\!\bra{0}$ and $\ket{1}\!\bra{1}$.

The second codeword set is a singleton, so its pairwise-collision hypothesis is
vacuous for every $\eta\geq0$.  The second marginal is exactly consistent, and
the perfectly correlated state makes the joint answer measurement exactly
self-consistent.  The first marginal differs from the constantly-zero
codeword answer precisely on the $\ket{1,1}$ component, so its consistency
defect is $\rho$.  Consequently all hypotheses of the pasting lemma hold with
$\delta=\rho$.

The pasted measurement also has a single codeword outcome and its effect is the
identity.  After evaluation it is deterministic at $(0,*)$, whereas the joint
answer measurement returns $(1,*)$ with probability $\rho$.  Their final
consistency defect is therefore $\rho$.  Thus the asserted conclusion would
require
\[
  \rho \leq c_{\rm out}\delta_{\mathrm{pasting}}(\eta,\rho)
  \qquad\text{for every }\eta>0.
\]
The product contract gives the opposite asymptotic bound
$\delta_{\mathrm{pasting}}(\eta,\rho)\leq C(\eta\rho)^C$.  Since $C>0$, the
right side, even multiplied by the fixed $c_{\rm out}$, tends to zero with
$\eta$, which is a contradiction. Here $c_{\rm in}=1$ suffices for all
three input comparisons. As $\rho$ can
be arbitrarily small, this failure is not confined to the large-error boundary.
It uses positive $\eta$ throughout: no extension of the printed scalar
bound to $\eta=0$ is needed. The very same zero-collision example satisfies
the hypotheses for every positive collision upper bound.
